What does Oregon require for a squatter to gain title by adverse possession?

A person must hold the land for 10 years in actual, open, notorious, exclusive, hostile and continuous possession, and must prove every element by clear and convincing evidence. That is the core of ORS 105.620, the statute that governs adverse possession of fee simple title in Oregon.

The statute adds an element many people overlook. At the moment of first entry, the possessor must have honestly believed they were the actual owner, and that belief needs an objective basis and must be reasonable under the circumstances. The belief has to last through the whole vesting period.

In plain terms, someone who walks into a vacant house knowing it belongs to somebody else has a hard road under this statute. The claim fits better in a boundary mix-up, a bad legal description, or a long run of occupancy under a defective deed.

  • Hostile possession means possession under a claim of right or with color of title.
  • Color of title means a claim under a written conveyance, or by operation of law from someone who claims under one.
  • Grazing livestock alone is not enough without further supporting facts.
  • The word person in the statute includes the state and its political subdivisions.

Oregon adverse possession and squatter rules at a glance

TopicWhat the source saysWhere it comes from
Possession period10 years, including predecessors in interestORS 105.620
Proof standardClear and convincing evidenceORS 105.620
Co-owner claim against other co-owners20 years of exclusive possession plus payment of all assessed taxesORS 105.615
Time limit to sue to recover real property10 yearsORS 12.050
Squatter notice to vacate24 hours, in writing2025 Oregon Laws chapter 356
Effective date of the squatter notice lawJanuary 1, 20262025 Oregon Laws chapter 356
Criminal trespass, second degreeClass C misdemeanorORS 164.245

Is an Oregon squatter the same thing as an adverse possessor?

No. A squatter is an occupant with no right to be there, while an adverse possessor is a squatter who has run out a 10 year clock and met every element of the statute.

Oregon wrote a definition of squatter into the landlord and tenant chapter in 2025. Under the new language added to ORS 90.100, a squatter is a person occupying a dwelling unit, or other property used for dwelling purposes, who is not entitled to be there under a rental agreement and was not authorized by a tenant. A tenant who holds over under ORS 90.427 is carved out of the definition.

That distinction matters for owners of inherited, vacant or tenant-abandoned houses. Most occupants who show up in a month or a year are trespassers, not claimants. The 10 year statute becomes a real concern only when an owner has ignored a property for a very long time.

How does Oregon's 24-hour squatter notice work?

An owner or landlord can give a squatter 24 hours' written notice to leave, then pursue possession in court if the person stays. House Bill 3522 was approved by the Governor on June 20, 2025, and took effect January 1, 2026, as chapter 356 of the 2025 Oregon Laws.

The notice must state the date and time to vacate and say the reason is the person's squatter status. It does not create any right of occupancy or tenancy. The law also added a new cause to ORS 105.115, so a squatter who stays past the notice is unlawfully holding by force.

  • The notice goes through the same court track used for eviction cases under ORS 105.100 to 105.168.
  • The eviction complaint form in ORS 105.126 now has a "24-hour notice for squatter" option.
  • The law sets an $88 filing fee under ORS 105.130 and applies dwelling unit procedures and fees to these cases.

Before this change, a legislative committee analysis described the problem as owners having to use slower tools. The 2025 bill passed the House Committee on Housing and Homelessness 10 to 0, with two members not voting, on March 24, 2025.

What happens in court after the notice expires?

The owner files a summons and complaint in the circuit court for the county where the house sits, and the clerk sets a first appearance. The Oregon Judicial Department's eviction help page says that first appearance usually falls about 7 to 15 days after filing, and a contested trial is usually set within 15 to 30 days after that.

If the owner wins, the clerk issues a notice of restitution. The occupant then has four days from service to move out. If the person stays, the owner returns to court for a writ of execution, and the sheriff schedules removal.

  • Only the sheriff may use physical force. Private help is not allowed.
  • The case covers possession only. Back rent or damages need a separate small claims action.
  • After removal, the owner must store the remaining belongings and give proper notice of the occupant's rights.

These steps come from the court's general residential eviction guide, written by Coos and Curry County courts. Local practice can vary, so ask the clerk of your county circuit court about its schedule and fees.

What other options does an Oregon owner have against an unauthorized occupant?

An owner can ask police to treat the occupant as a trespasser, sue for possession in an ejectment action, or negotiate a voluntary exit. Each has limits, and the best path depends on how the person got in.

Criminal trespass in the second degree covers a person who enters or remains unlawfully in or upon premises. It is a Class C misdemeanor under ORS 164.245. The Oregon Property Owners Association notes, in an April 2024 article written before the new notice law, that police are not required to act and may call a dispute a civil matter if the occupant claims a right to be there.

Ejectment is the older civil route. ORS 105.005 lets a person with a legal estate in real property and a present right to possess it recover possession, plus damages, from whoever is in possession. The same article warns that contested ejectment cases can be slow and expensive.

  • Forcible entry law starts from a basic rule in ORS 105.105: no one may enter land unless the right of entry is given by law, and entry must be peaceable.
  • If a squatter leaves, the same article says the owner may reoccupy, and should call police if the person returns.
  • Self-help carries risk, so many owners involve an attorney before changing locks.

Can an heir or co-owner claim an Oregon house by adverse possession?

Yes, but the bar is higher. A co-owner holding as a tenant in common can acquire the whole title against other co-owners after 20 years of exclusive possession, and only if that person paid all taxes assessed during that period (ORS 105.615).

The possessing co-owner does not have to notify the others. The rule applies unless a granting document or agreement says otherwise. Court decisions summarized on the statute page say periods of possession by different co-owners cannot be added together, and that title vests as a matter of law when the prerequisites are met at the end of the period.

This is the version of the issue that shows up in inherited houses. A sibling who lives in the family home for decades, pays the tax bill and shuts out the others may build a claim. Siblings who live elsewhere should know the clock is real.

How does a squatter or title cloud affect selling an Oregon house?

An occupant with no lease, or an open claim to the land, can delay a sale until it is resolved. A buyer will want clear possession at closing.

Owners in this spot usually face one of three situations.

  • A person is in the house with no agreement, and the notice process above is the main route to possession.
  • A neighbor or former occupant claims part of the lot, and the dispute may need a court judgment or a recorded agreement before title is clean.
  • Heirs disagree about who owns what, and a co-owner has been living there alone.

We buy houses as-is. An attorney or the title company can tell you what must be settled before a closing date. To weigh a cash offer against the time and cost of a court case, send us the address and a short description.

Which Oregon courts and offices handle these cases?

Possession actions are filed in the circuit court of the county where the property sits, and Oregon has 36 counties, with Multnomah the most populous. Each county clerk can explain local filing steps, fee deferral forms and hearing calendars.

Deed records, including any recorded agreement that fixes a boundary or releases a claim, go to the county clerk or recording office. In Multnomah County, for example, the base fee to record a deed is $86 for the first page and $5 for each added page. Other counties set their own fees, so check before you send documents.

Read the current text of ORS chapters 90, 105 and 12 before you act, and talk to an Oregon attorney about your facts.

Frequently asked questions

How many years does adverse possession take in Oregon?

Ten years of actual, open, notorious, exclusive, hostile and continuous possession under ORS 105.620, and the possessor must also have honestly and reasonably believed they owned the land. Co-owners claiming against each other need 20 years plus payment of all taxes under ORS 105.615.

Can I remove a squatter from my Oregon house in 24 hours?

You can give a 24-hour written notice, but removal still requires a court case if the person stays. Since January 1, 2026, the notice is the first step, and only the sheriff can carry out removal after a judgment, notice of restitution and writ.

Does a squatter need to pay property taxes to win in Oregon?

For ordinary adverse possession under ORS 105.620, the statute text does not list tax payment as an element. For a co-owner claiming against other co-owners under ORS 105.615, paying all assessed taxes is required.

Is trespassing a crime in Oregon?

Yes. Entering or remaining unlawfully in or upon premises is criminal trespass in the second degree, a Class C misdemeanor under ORS 164.245. Police may still treat a dispute as a civil matter if the occupant claims a right to be there.

Can I sell my Oregon house if someone is living there without permission?

You can, but possession usually has to be resolved before a buyer or title company will close. Cash buyers can buy as-is, though the closing still depends on delivering the property as agreed.

Which Oregon law governs landlords and tenants?

Most residential rentals in Oregon fall under chapter 90 of the Oregon Revised Statutes, the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Mobile home and floating home parks have their own section of that chapter, and some rules, such as the rent cap, state that they do not apply there.

Cities can add to the state rules. Portland, for example, requires landlords to pay relocation assistance in several situations and an annotation to ORS 90.427 notes that the state section does not preempt local relocation ordinances (Owen v. City of Portland, 2020). A landlord selling a rental should check both layers before giving any notice.

How much can an Oregon landlord raise the rent?

Oregon caps yearly rent increases for most tenancies, and the percentage is published each year by the state. The Department of Administrative Services announced 9.5 percent for 2026 and 10 percent for 2027, calculated as the lesser of 10 percent or 7 percent plus the consumer price index for tenancies covered by ORS 90.323.

The same statute sets process rules.

  • Written notice at least 90 days before the increase takes effect, or 7 days for a week-to-week tenancy.
  • No increase during the first year of a tenancy that is not week-to-week.
  • No more than one increase in any 12-month period.
  • The notice must state the amount, the new rent and the effective date.

Buildings are exempt from the cap if the first certificate of occupancy was issued less than 15 years before the notice. Regulated affordable housing has its own exemption. A landlord who breaks the cap owes the tenant three months of rent plus actual damages. See the state rent stabilization page for the current figure.

What fees and late charges can a landlord charge?

Oregon allows only the fees that ORS 90.302 and ORS 90.260 list, and each one has to appear in the written rental agreement. A landlord who charges a prohibited fee owes the tenant twice the actual damages or $300, whichever is greater.

ChargeLimit in the statute
Late rent, flat feeOne reasonable flat amount per rental period, once rent is not received by the fourth day
Late rent, daily feeStarts on day 5, no more than 6 percent of the flat fee per day
Late rent, percentage fee5 percent of periodic rent for each five-day period or part of one
Tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarmUp to $250
Abandoning a fixed-term tenancyUp to 1.5 times monthly rent
Repeated rule violationsMostly capped at $50, with prior written warnings; smoking and unauthorized dangerous pets capped at $250

Unpaid late fees cannot be the basis for a nonpayment termination, although they can support a for-cause termination. A landlord who changes the late fee structure in a periodic tenancy must give 30 days of written notice. The sources are ORS 90.260 and ORS 90.302.

What are the rules on security deposits?

A landlord must return a security deposit, or give an itemized written accounting for what is kept, within 31 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant delivers possession. The rule is in ORS 90.300, and it also covers last month's rent deposits.

  • A landlord may keep only what is reasonably necessary for unpaid rent, other defaults, and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear.
  • After the first year of tenancy, a landlord generally cannot require a new or increased deposit, apart from specific cases such as agreeing to allow a pet.
  • A pet deposit cannot be charged for a service animal or companion animal that a tenant with a disability needs as a reasonable accommodation.
  • A landlord who misses the deadline or withholds in bad faith owes the tenant twice the amount withheld.

For a seller, the statute also says the person who holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends answers to the tenant for the deposit. Deposits and prepaid rent should be tracked and credited in the closing paperwork so the new owner is not surprised.

What counts as retaliation by a landlord?

After a tenant takes a protected action, an Oregon landlord cannot raise rent, cut services, serve a termination notice or file or threaten a possession case in response. ORS 90.385 lists the protected actions.

  • Complaining to a government agency about a code violation that affects health or safety.
  • Making a good-faith complaint to the landlord about the tenancy.
  • Joining or organizing a tenants' union.
  • Testifying against the landlord in a court, agency or legislative proceeding.
  • Winning a possession case within the previous six months, unless the win came only from improper service or too little notice.

The statute gives the landlord some exceptions, such as a complaint made in an unreasonable manner or a tenant who was behind on rent when the notice was served. Retaliation is also a defense the tenant can raise in a possession case, which is why a notice served soon after a complaint deserves a second look before a sale is planned around it.

What can a landlord do about showings and repairs?

A landlord must keep the unit habitable under ORS 90.320, and may enter to inspect, repair, supply services or show the unit to prospective buyers under ORS 90.322. The two duties run together when a rental is on the market.

Habitability includes weather protection, plumbing, hot and cold running water, adequate heat, electrical lighting, safe grounds, garbage receptacles, floors, walls and stairs in good repair, and a working smoke alarm at the start of the tenancy.

Landlord insurance rules are in ORS 90.222. If a landlord requires renter's liability insurance, it must be in the written agreement, the landlord must carry comparable coverage and show proof on request, and a month-to-month tenant gets at least 30 days of written notice before the requirement is added.

Does Portland add its own tenant protections?

Yes. Portland requires a landlord to pay mandatory relocation assistance to a tenant in several situations, including a no-cause termination, a qualifying landlord reason for ending a tenancy, a rent increase of 10 percent or more in 12 months, and a substantial change in lease terms.

Unit sizeRelocation payment
Studio or single room occupancy$2,900
One bedroom$3,300
Two bedrooms$4,200
Three bedrooms or larger$4,500

The landlord pays, the tenant must get at least 90 days of written notice that describes the right, and the landlord has 30 days to report each payment to the Portland Housing Bureau. A landlord who does not comply can owe up to three times the monthly rent plus actual damages, the relocation amount and attorney fees. Exemptions exist and most require a filing, so read the city's relocation page before relying on one.

How should a landlord handle tenants when selling the rental?

Among the qualifying landlord reasons in ORS 90.427, a sale counts only when the buyer intends in good faith to live in the home. ORS 90.300 makes whoever holds the landlord's interest answerable for the deposit, and ORS 90.427 limits when a month-to-month tenancy can be ended after the first year.

  • Settle the deposit and prepaid rent in writing.
  • Give showing notice that follows ORS 90.322.
  • Check any rent increase notice against the 90-day and once-a-year limits.
  • If a qualifying reason applies, such as a buyer who will live in the home, follow the notice and payment steps in our eviction guide and pay attention to the three-month penalty for a wrongful termination.

Some owners prefer to skip those steps and sell to a buyer who will keep the tenant in place. We buy houses with tenants in Oregon, and you can ask us what that looks like for your lease.

Frequently asked questions

How much can my landlord raise my rent in Oregon?

The cap for 2026 is 9.5 percent and for 2027 it is 10 percent, for tenancies covered by ORS 90.323. The landlord must give 90 days of written notice, cannot raise rent in the first year, and can raise it only once in 12 months. Buildings under 15 years old are exempt.

How soon must a landlord return a security deposit in Oregon?

Within 31 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant gives up possession. The landlord must return the deposit or send an itemized written accounting. A landlord who withholds in bad faith can owe twice the amount withheld.

Can a landlord charge a late fee in Oregon?

Yes, but only if the written rental agreement provides for it and rent is not received by the fourth day of the rental period. The fee must be one of the three structures in ORS 90.260, either a flat fee, a daily fee starting on day 5, or 5 percent of rent per five-day period.

Does a new owner have to honor an existing lease in Oregon?

ORS 90.300 says the holder of the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends answers to the tenant for the deposit, and ORS 90.427 limits ending a tenancy early to listed reasons with set notice. Ask an attorney how those rules apply to your lease.

Is Portland relocation assistance required when I sell?

Only if a triggering event applies, such as a qualifying landlord reason for ending the tenancy, and no exemption covers you. The amounts run from $2,900 for a studio to $4,500 for three bedrooms or larger, and the tenant needs at least 90 days of notice.
